reconcile.connective: Gill argues both timelines are literally true: the merchants driven out on the day of the triumphal entry (per Matthew) simply returned overnight and were expelled a second time the next morning (per Mark).

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells's Skeptic's Annotated Bible catalogs the two timelines side by side as a flat, unresolved contradiction over whether the fig tree was cursed before or after the temple was cleared.

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, Skeptic's Annotated Bible (1999), contra/fig_temple.html

excerpts.excerpt_text: …which was done, as Matthew relates, the same day that he made his public entry into Jerusalem: wherefore it is highly probable, that upon Christ's leaving the city, they returned "again", and were the next morning sitting and doing business in the temple as before; and were drove out again by Christ, who, upon his return, found them there.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Gill directly reconciles Matthew's same-day temple cleansing with Mark's next-morning cleansing by positing a second, unrecorded expulsion: the merchants returned overnight and were driven out again the day Mark places the episode relative to the fig-tree curse.

pd_work.resource: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63)
pd_work.author: John Gill
pd_work.note: Gill's own note on Mark 11:15 treats this exact passage, proposing the temple was cleared twice: once as Matthew records it on the day of the triumphal entry, and again the next morning as Mark records it, after the merchants had returned overnight.

link.title: GotQuestions: Why did Jesus curse the fig tree?
link.note: explicitly contrasts Matthew's single combined account (fig tree cursed and withered after the temple cleansing) with Mark's two-day sequence (fig tree cursed before the cleansing, withering discovered the next day)
